t: Why Instilling A Love Of School Should Be Your Highest Priority
q: If you were to have only one goal this coming school year, make it that your students enjoy being in your classroom.
Instilling a love for school affects and changes students like nothing else can or ever will, improving the effectiveness of virtually everything you do.
The unavoidable truth is that when boredom and dissatisfaction take root in your classroom, your students will create their own enjoyment.
Like poison ivy amid the world’s changing climates, disrespect and misbehavior thrive in such an environment.
It is simply an attitude, a spirit, and a cultivation of enjoyment. It’s finding humor in the everyday and laughter for laughter’s sake.
The sad result is that the life and vitality of the classroom becomes lost in a forest of peripherals.
x: No classroom management strategy motivates behavior and academic focus as powerfully as students genuinely enjoying being in the classroom.

t: Why You Should Take Your Time The First Few Weeks Of School eks-of-school/
q: No matter what you hear from your colleagues, no matter how far they say they’ve gotten into the curriculum, or how they’re already working in groups or rotating students through centers, avoid the temptation to join them.

It pays, you see, to get it right the first time around. It pays to take a deliberate approach, to teach the details, the ins and outs, and the A to Zs of being a polite, successful, and contributing member of your classroom.
You watch aghast as your students begin stepping out of line to goof and jostle with their friends, shout out to little brothers or big sisters, and disrupt the working classrooms lining the hallway.
Because early in the school year an occasional breakdown in behavior is expected. No teacher escapes the first few weeks without being tested or tried or disappointed.
Once you convince your class that when you say it they can take it to the bank, everything becomes much, much easier.
Hold them to it and they’ll learn. Take them back to the scene of the crime and give them a chance to fix it and they will.
x: Avoid rushing to match colleagues who seem further ahead in curriculum or student independence early in the year.

t: How Administrators Can Wage War on Bad PD
q: Whoever's doing the talking is doing the thinking.” Good PD should involve a mixture of a leader talking and participants talking. Any PD that is 100% presented content probably involves someone selling you something and probably won't impact your teachers.
Teachers don't like cutesy, and activity for activity's sake is cutesy.

In my experience, the best homegrown PD involves getting into each others' classrooms and processing what's working and what's not. Yet, due to scheduling and space constraints, this is pretty impractical to do on a large scale.

We watched and discussed three videos that day; it was so refreshing to see teachers we knew doing moves we had learned about. There was nothing flashy, no professional video editing — just teachers watching/discussing teaching.

But it's seriously important to teachers that the person presenting to them understands what it's like to manage a full course load with bloated class sizes and testing pressures and helicopter parents and free/reduced lunch issues and national standards movements.
If the PD person you're looking at has no track record of results to share upon request, your teachers are likely to sense that this person is selling a soft hard-boiled egg.
Some of the brightest researchers and writers in the world are absolutely horrible presenters — just watch a TED talk.
x: Good PD needs participants talking, not just a presenter delivering content, and each mode of interaction should be chosen with intent rather than for variety's sake.

t: How To Avoid A Bad Start To Your School Year https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/08/17/how-to-avoid-a-bad-start-to-your-school-year/
q: But just below the surface there is a danger lurking, a danger that can lullaby even the most vigilant teachers to sleep at the wheel.
If you look close, lo about the third week of school, you’ll notice a smidgen of sloppiness in the way your students line up for lunch or turn in their homework or gather themselves into groups.

And so they'll remind. They'll warn and threaten. They'll harp and harangue on the importance of listening, performing routines, and giving a good effort. But for the most part, it falls on deaf ears.
The strategy is this: Never move on until you’re getting exactly what you want from your students.
Usually, this takes nothing more than a pause. Other times, though, you may have to stop them in their tracks, rewind to the beginning, and start again.
When you steadfastly refuse to continue on and on, unsatisfied and unhappy with what you’re seeing in your students, there is no telling what can be accomplished.

Refusing to move forward until standards are met yields maximum time-on-task, confidence, and staggering long-term progress.

The core strategy: never transition, start a lesson, or continue an activity until students are meeting the exact standard set for them.

t: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 6 — Write Like Crazy
q: One of the biggest bang-for-your-buck Common Core standards is W.CCR.10, which basically says, “Write frequently for many reasons.” And the amazing thing about writing is that it achieves so many things simultaneously.

One thing I would say not to do is simply tell kids to read Chapter 13, Section 2, and answer all of the questions at the back of the book. The questions and activities provided with textbooks are often designed by people who have never taught, and they are generally low- to zero-effective in helping kids become better readers, writers, and thinkers.

Instead, create your own response questions that are interesting and simple; these questions, like the examples above, should be along the lines of reading between the lines (inferring), arguing, making connections to other content, or drawing conclusions.

If you just do this — add writing to every reading task — and if you give kids one to two opportunities minimum to read complex texts every week, I'd be shocked not to see some serious gains in your kids in the areas of reading and writing.
He went on to say that his students never know which of their pieces he's going to read, so they stay on their toes while he stays sane.
The length of these papers should increase with each grade level, and the bulk of the work should be done in class so we can walk around checking for understanding and ensuring student success.

The key for content area teachers is to remember that we are not English teachers — we're aiming for clarity and content, as Mike Schmoker says, as well as the ability to cite written sources to support arguments or conclusions with evidence.

t: Waging War on the Bad Guys
q: And before I share who the bad guys are in my opinion, let me just state that I love focusing on problems I can tackle, and I despise focusing on problems I can't touch.
At the same time, I hate focusing on problems like “the public has a low opinion of teachers.” It's one of those problems where, the more you whine about it the worse it's actually going to get.

As McShane points out, anyone can put a Common Core sticker on a textbook or a Teachers Pay Teachers lesson. The resulting over-abundance of non-Common-Core-aligned “Common Core aligned” stuff is a veritable nightmare.
It's simple. It's proven. It empowers teachers with a working knowledge of the Core.

And let's be honest: part of this is our fault as teachers. I swear that, for some of my friends, if Jesus himself walked in and led a professional development session, the second he was done they'd be like, “Well, that's easy for him to say — he's retired.
I'm not saying any of this is easy; I'm just saying it's something we have the power to influence. It's a dragon we can make swords for.

t: 6 Things You Must Do On The First Day Of School
q: You have one opportunity to start your school year on the right classroom management foot, one shot to propel your first day of school into the best learning experience your students have ever had.
Your initial friendliness and open, welcoming heart will put them at ease and spark an immediate desire to please you, follow your lead, and pay forward your kindness throughout the classroom.
This first routine, when taught with depth and precision, and then practiced successfully, paves the way for all other routines to be learned quickly and thereafter performed with excellence.
You’re going to promise them that you will protect their special community, that you will protect their right to learn and enjoy school.
Establish from the get-go that your classroom is in the business of learning by diving into a challenging academic lesson (or two or three) on the first day of school.
Have your content, your objectives, and the overall tone of the day pictured clearly in your mind, but allow yourself room to mess up, to stumble over your words.
x: Promise to protect students' right to learn and enjoy school, then follow through by teaching the classroom management plan as a safeguard, not a punishment system.
Build rapport immediately by greeting students warmly and signaling they're now part of a unique classroom community.
Model one key routine (such as morning entry) with excellent, step-by-step precision to set a template for how all future routines will be taught.
